title: KV & prefix cache hit-rate modeling, TTL tuning, and safe rollout playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: Produce concrete, production-ready recommendations for KV/prefix caching that balance cost savings from batching with correctness and availability. Deliverables: (1) hit-rate modeling approach and a small simulator that uses request traces to estimate marginal token-savings for different cache sizes and key designs, (2) TTL and eviction policy guidelines tuned for interactive vs. background workloads, (3) cache-key design patterns to avoid pollution and enable reuse across model variants, and (4) a safe apply/rollback playbook (canary %, SLO triggers, automated rollback conditions, and observability knobs).
background: Recent experiments show that prefix/KV caching combined with smarter batching reduces per-token GPU work by up to 22% on conversational workloads, but naive TTLs and overly-broad cache keys caused correctness edge cases and cache pollution in staging. We need reproducible modeling and a deployment playbook so teams can enable cache configs safely across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
proposal:
1) Hit-rate modeling: Build an empirical estimator that consumes request traces (user_id, model, prompt_prefix_hash, sequence_length) and computes: estimated hit rate as a function of cache size (N entries) and key granularity; marginal token-savings = expected avoided kv-ops * average kv-cost-per-token. Use a two-step approach: (a) offline trace sampler + LRU simulation to produce hit-rate curves, (b) lightweight production sampler that logs prefix fingerprints to estimate live hit-rate without storing payloads.

2) Key design: Recommend namespaced keys: <customer_id>:<model_family>:<prefix_hash>:<session_bucket>. Use prefix hashing with collision-resistant 64-bit non-cryptographic hashes and include model-qualifier to avoid cross-model leaks. For shared templates (e.g., system prompts), allow a public prefix namespace to increase reuse.

3) TTL & policy tuning: Classify workloads into interactive (low-latency, high churn) and background/batching (higher reuse). Interactive: short TTLs (30s–2m) + sticky LRU to favor recent sessions. Background: longer TTLs (30m–6h) with size-based eviction. Provide guidance for token-aware TTL: scale TTL by prefix reuse score computed from traces.

4) Safe apply & rollback: Canary rollout with gradual enablement: 0.5% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% traffic. Monitor metrics at 1m and 5m cadence: cache_hit_rate, tokens_saved_per_min, p95_latency_change, model_response_drift (via z-scored eval set), downstream error rate. Automated rollback triggers: drop in cached hit rate > 30% from baseline, p95 latency increase > 20% or model_response_drift exceeding threshold. Implement feature-flagged config with enforced kill-switch and automated policy to revert to per-request mode if rollback triggers fire.
acceptance_criteria: Offline simulator accepts N= {10K, 50K, 200K} entry sizes and produces hit-rate curves and marginal token-savings for at least three representative traces (chat, single-shot generation, reranking)
TTL guidelines documented with numeric recommendations for interactive vs background workloads and example config snippets for Hosted/Dedicated/Private
Cache key patterns documented with examples, anti-patterns, and migration notes (how to rotate keys safely)
Canary rollout runbook checked into ops-playbooks with automated dashboards and defined rollback checks and Slack pager hooks
Proof-of-concept deployment in staging with A/B: observed token cost reduction >= 12% for chat trace without measurable correctness regressions on eval prompts
